articles.title: These Raspberry Pi price hikes are no joke
articles.summary: Raspberry Pi is raising its prices again due to RAM price hikes and launching a 3GB version of the Pi 4, which it says isn’t an April Fool’s joke.
articles.body: As of today, the price of the 16GB version of the Raspberry Pi 5 is going up by $100, a price bump that’s almost as much as the original $120 price tag. Driven by the ongoing RAM shortage, Raspberry Pi is raising prices on over a dozen of its bare-bones computers, after previous increases in December and February. The increases range from $11.25 to $150. In a blog post announcing the price increases, Raspberry Pi CEO Eben Upton reiterated that they won’t be permanent, stating, “The circumstances in which we find ourselves are challenging, but in the future they will abate. When they do, we will reverse our price increases, and until they do, we will continue to work hard to limit their impact in every way we can.” To potentially soften the blow of the price hikes, Raspberry Pi also announced a new version of the Raspberry Pi 4 with 3GB of RAM available starting today, priced at $83.75. Raspberry Pi models with 4GB or more of memory have been impacted the most by memory price surges. Upton also notes that it’s not an April Fools’ stunt, adding, “Notwithstanding today’s date, our new computer is as real as the rest of our products.”

articles.title: AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon team up to eliminate coverage dead zones
articles.summary: AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon have agreed to work together under a new joint venture that aims to end wireless dead zones in the US.
articles.body: AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon have agreed to work together under a new joint venture that aims to end wireless dead zones in the US. The partnership was announced today as an “agreement in principle,” but if finalized would see the three carrier companies pooling their ground-based spectrum resources together to increase coverage in rural areas. The goal is to create the “best and most diverse ecosystem for wireless and satellite products and services,” though details on how this will actually be achieved are fairly vague. There’s mention of the venture developing a unified technical standard for customers and satellite network operators, and investing in satellite-based, direct-to-device (D2D) technologies to address coverage gaps and improve connectivity. In its press release, AT&T says that existing carrier-satellite agreements will remain in place under this proposed joint venture. “Our goal is to make staying connected simple, no matter where you are — on a rural highway, in a national park, on a boat, or during an emergency,” AT&T CEO John Stankey said in a statement. “By joining with other carriers, we’re bringing our combined expertise to accelerate our customers’ access to reliable, and always-on coverage everywhere.” The joint venture is still subject to closing conditions and negotiations between AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon. If this does go ahead, however, the outcome will theoretically be good for everyone. Customers should get access to stronger, more reliable connectivity in areas that struggled with mobile service, and satellite services can more easily serve folks in areas that traditional cell networks can’t cover.

articles.title: This very fancy e-bike is one of the first to go semi-solid state
articles.summary: The Lemmo 3 e-bike is a longtail cargo, and one of the first electric bikes to feature a semi-solid state battery that’s less prone to thermal runaway.
articles.body: The Lemmo 3 is the first cargo bike from the respected German e-bike maker. This premium, step-through longtail is a slightly less insane take on Rivian’s Also TM-B, with one major advantage: It’s one of the first electric bikes to feature a semi-solid state battery. Semi-solid state batteries are far safer than traditional lithium-ion batteries. Their gel-like composition offers improved energy density, with far less risk of thermal runaway. That translates to improved range and longevity from a more compact battery that’s unlikely to catch fire when left charging overnight in your house or business. The semi-solid state electrolyte even remains stable when punctured in a crash. [Media: The Lemmo 3 is fitted with a massive 960Wh battery promising up to 180km (110 miles) of range. And by going with a semi-solid state chemistry, the company claims the battery is 20 percent smaller and lighter while still offering 30 percent longer lifespan. The removable battery can also power your AC appliances (up to 1000W) and USB-C devices (up to 66W) once you arrive at your destination, similar to Cake’s now-defunct Ösa. [Image: The Lemmo 3 battery plugged into Lemmo’s optional V2L Discharge Inverter that costs an extra €169. The Lemmo 3 is being marketed as an eSUV just like the Amflow TL Carbon I reviewed. But this very heavy full suspension cargo bike will feel more comfortable on daily commutes to daycare, work, and stores than weekend single tracks. The bike weighs 39kg (86 pounds) with the 5kg (11 pound) battery installed. Instead of doing something proprietary, Lemmo made its longtail compatible with MIK HD accessories. These include a wide variety of child seats, bags, and boxes that can be mounted on the rear rack. It can handle a 200kg (441lb) total load, with 80kg (176lbs) supported in the rear and 20kg (44lbs) on the front rack. A quick-adjust saddle and handlebar makes the Lemmo 3 easily shareable, supporting riders from 155cm (5 feet 1 inch) to 195cm (6 feet 5 inches). The bike is fitted with wide tires on a 24-inch front wheel paired with a smaller 20-inch wheel in the back. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Powering this beast is a rear-hub motor (750W in the US, 500W Canada, 250W for Europe). It can deliver up to 90Nm of torque to get heavy loads rolling or to help surmount hills. Naturally, there’s AI baked in as well. The motor and e-derailleur combine data from a variety of sensors to “feed an adaptive Al model that selects the optimal gear in real time, creating a natural, responsive, and effortless ride.” That sounds expensive to fix when the drivetrain eventually needs servicing. The motor can also be paired with a 3-speed auto-shifting gearbox and belt drive for flatter environments. Other features include fully integrated lighting (with turn signals and brake lights), a 3.5-inch touchscreen, a USB-C port to charge your phone, OTA updates, rear-facing radar to alert you of approaching vehicles, and hydraulic brakes that apply stopping power to both wheels simultaneously when pulling just one brake lever. Security features include embedded frame and battery locks and GPS / LTE tracking. The Lemmo 3 already has a teaser page up on Kickstarter that says “launching soon” for the EU, UK, US, and Canada. You can reserve it now for a refundable deposit of €39.90, which locks you into tax-exclusive pricing of €1,890 (or about $2,155). The company says retail pricing will climb well beyond €3,390 (over $3,800). Lemmo is targeting first deliveries for April 2027.

articles.title: Huawei made a whole camera to attach to its latest phone
articles.summary: This 24–240mm zoom lens has its own sensor too.
articles.body: Over the last few years, Chinese Android manufacturers have followed Vivo’s example of launching add-on “teleconverter” lenses for their flagship phones, enabling long-distance photography that the phones on their own could never match. Today, Huawei one-upped everybody with the add-on lens for its Mate 90 Pro Max flagship, which is not only a comically huge zoom lens, but also includes its own image sensor. The 1-inch-type, 50-megapixel RYYB sensor inside the Ruiying Z10 is bigger than any inside the phone itself, so attaching this lens doesn’t just give you better glass, it’s actually a complete overhaul of the camera capabilities. And while other teleconverters have so far had fixed focal lengths, this is a true zoom lens that covers 24–240mm, with a variable aperture of f/2.0-f/4.5. This is almost a camera in its own right, only using the phone for power, processing, and software. [Image: Impressively, Huawei also appears to have designed the lens to attach directly to compatible phones, instead of needing an intermediary case for a mounting point. The obvious downside to the Z10 is that it’s absolutely enormous, even by teleconverter standards — you’re not going to fit this thing in your pocket. But at 346g, it’s still smaller and more portable than even most mirrorless cameras, and you’ll probably be able to take it into venues where cameras aren’t permitted, like concerts and sports matches. Then there’s the price: at ¥5,999 (around $895), this is more expensive than some flagship phones. Huawei says the Z10 is compatible with the collector’s edition of the Mate 90 Pro Max and its Mate 90 RS variant, the only two models in the new Mate 90 series with the screw-mount around the camera island. They have impressive cameras in their own right, with an f/1.4-f/4.0, 50-megapixel, variable aperture main camera using a 1.1.28-inch-type sensor; a 200-megapixel 4x periscope telephoto with the same size sensor; and a 40-megapixel ultrawide. The 6.9-inch OLED display can hit 12,000 nits of peak brightness, and it’s powered by a 6,800mAh battery and Huawei’s own Kirin 9050 Pro chip. The Mate 90 and Mate 90 Pro are both slightly smaller, with streamlined specs across the board. [Image: The Mate P90 Pro Max has a pretty nifty design too. Update, October 1st: Added the Z10’s price.

articles.title: HP’s answer to the MacBook Neo is thinner, lighter, and comes with OLED
articles.summary: The HP OmniBook 5 14 looks like a Neo wannabe right down to its 8GB of RAM and colors, but it seems a compelling competitor thanks in part to its OLED display.
articles.body: HP is announcing a new laptop that’s squarely aimed at Apple’s MacBook Neo. The 2026 HP OmniBook 5 14 starts at $699.99 with an Intel Core 5 315 “Wildcat Lake” processor, 8GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. Much of that sounds pretty familiar, being in lockstep with both Apple’s Neo and its recent competition from Dell, Asus, and Acer — the HP even offers a similar four color options in silver, pink, blue, and green. But one thing that separates the OmniBook is its inclusion of an OLED display on all configs. The OmniBook 5 14 can be configured much higher, with up to a Core 7 350 chip, 16GB of RAM, and a 1TB SSD, but all models include a 1080p webcam, dual speakers, HDMI, 3.5mm audio jack, and just two 10Gbps USB-C ports. And while the inclusion of OLED across the range is a major draw to the new OmniBook, the base config only has a passable 1920 x 1200 resolution and 300 nits of max brightness on its non-touch panel. A touchscreen version will be available when the OmniBook 5 launches in October, but a version with a 2560 x 1600 resolution OLED and 400 nits of brightness isn’t coming until March 2027. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: While the OmniBook 5 14 doesn’t seem poised to best the MacBook Neo in raw processing power (based on our other reviews of Wildcat Lake laptops) or screen brightness, it’s quite thin, light, and colorful. HP even gave it the nicer, sleeker lid logo usually reserved for pricier models. It starts at just 2.56 pounds, and it’s as thin as 0.46 inches / 11.7mm. That’s slightly lighter and thinner than a Neo. And I’d expect its Wildcat Lake chips to offer some good-to-great battery life. But we’ll have to see how it delivers in actual testing. Alongside the OmniBook 5 14, HP is also announcing a new ProBook 4 G2iS business laptop that it claims at 0.47 inches / 12mm is its “thinnest business notebook.” It’ll also start with Intel Wildcat Lake chips, 8GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD when it launches in December, but there’s no price yet. articles.title: The NYC Council’s marathon e-bike hearing seemed like a waste of time.
articles.summary:
The hearing, ostensibly on a massive package of 21 bills pertaining to e-bike safety, lasted approximately seven hours — but amounted to very little. According to Hell Gate:
> Perhaps the hearing’s lack of substance was due to the middling quality of the legislation itself, a hodgepodge of basic street safety actions (installing calming measures in bike lanes), cries for the state to do something (require e-bike riders to be registered), and increased app-based surveillance of deliveristas. But you can’t deny there were numerous bills. City Council Speaker Julie Menin touted the number as a “record” for a single hearing.
The anti-e-bike crowd was there, too, booing any mention of cars and trucks as the cause of the overwhelming majority of traffic crashes. What a productive use of everyone’s time!
[Link: E-Bike Sound and Fury, Signifying Nothing | https://hellgatenyc.com/e-bike-sound-and-fury-signifying-nothing/ | Hell Gate]

articles.title: Inside Microsoft’s big Copilot rethink
articles.summary: Copilot is now being positioned as the ‘OS for work.’
articles.body: Last week, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hosted an intimate, invite-only event for leaders from some of its key enterprise customers. Instead of a flashy media event, Nadella outlined the future of Copilot directly to the customers Microsoft really cares about, pitching its latest rethink of the AI assistant as the “OS for work.” Microsoft is adding coding and agent capabilities directly into Copilot, as well as bringing the full power of Office into Copilot for the first time. Nadella is betting that AI will change the way people work in the same way that Microsoft Office did in the ’80s and ’90s. “How did a multinational company do a forecast in 1981? You had interoffice memos and faxes and all of these artifacts that then just disappeared and you suddenly had an Excel spreadsheet in an email,” said Nadella. “We are the architects of a new frontier of work, using these new tools and capabilities.” Microsoft has spent the past few months fusing together its consumer and enterprise Copilot apps into a single unified user interface, with a goal to make Copilot as influential as Office once was. The result is a big departure from the Copilot consumer design that Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman launched two years ago. That design was heavily influenced by the work Inflection AI had done with the Pi personal AI assistant, after Microsoft hired many of the Inflection AI team just months prior. The new Copilot app now looks a lot more like the commercial one, with separate tabs for chat, coding, and the new Autopilot AI agent. There are some small nods to the consumer UI that was available before, but overall it looks like the type of enterprise app you’d associate with Microsoft. “There’s a really important reason why we decided to do this,” said Copilot chief Jacob Andreou at Microsoft’s customer-only event last week. “The bar for enterprise software is higher than it has ever been before. The expectations we have of the tools we adopt at work are set by the things we use after hours and at the weekends at home. What this means is that consumer UX and care needs to make its way into the workplace.” Andreou joined Microsoft AI last year, focused on product and growth. In March, Nadella appointed him as the single boss of Copilot across both commercial and consumer, reporting directly to the Microsoft CEO. He’s now responsible for the design, engineering, and growth of Copilot. Sources familiar with Microsoft’s Copilot plans tell me that redesigning Copilot over the last six months hasn’t been easy. There have been tensions between the team under Andreou, and those working for Charles Lamanna on the Copilot, Agents, and Platform (CAP) team. Lamanna’s team has been building Microsoft Scout, an always-on personal agent built on top of OpenClaw. Microsoft announced Scout at its Build developer conference in June, with just a desktop preview app. Less than six months later, I understand that the app has been put into maintenance mode, with Microsoft focusing on the cloud version, which has been rebranded to Autopilot. I’m told the rebrand was driven in part by legal concerns around the Scout name, as Yahoo uses “Yahoo Scout” branding for its own AI-powered features. Sources tell me Microsoft had even considered using Mico, the Clippy-like character from the consumer Copilot, to replace Scout. Nadella favored Autopilot instead, allowing Microsoft to present its AI agent in a more enterprise-friendly way, instead of a bouncing blob. Some of Microsoft’s caution around making Autopilot too cute comes at a time when rogue AI agents are hacking into businesses. Nadella addressed these concerns last week, laying out Microsoft’s design goals for Copilot. “[It’s] about organizations having control of their firms in an age of AI, where AI by definition is a learning machine,” said Nadella. “It can’t be about leaking the core of what your firm is about.” Andreou also admitted that agents “have been almost impossible to bring into the enterprise,” due to them needing the autonomy and flexibility that businesses usually balk at. “It is their superpower, and it’s the same thing that makes them absolutely terrifying to an IT admin.” Microsoft thinks it has solved the AI agent problem for businesses with its “OS for work,” but it also seems to be leaving the door open for competitors like Meta and OpenAI to build the “OS for life.” In a world where 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT every week, Microsoft is playing to its traditional business-focused strengths instead of trying to compete with consumer-friendly Muse and Dots agents. Andreou isn’t giving up on Copilot for consumers just yet, however, and he seems to want to hone in on those that want the power of enterprise apps at home. “Microsoft consumers are a little bit special. There’s almost 90 million folks that pay for Microsoft 365 out of their own pocket,” said Andreou. “These are people who value the use of things like PowerPoint and Excel so much in their personal lives that they actually go ahead and pay for it themselves.” With Office baked into Copilot, you’ll soon be able to create and edit inside Microsoft’s AI assistant instead of having to switch to Office apps like Word and PowerPoint. There’s a full ribbon interface, and it essentially looks like the web version of Office directly inside Copilot. I think this is Microsoft’s first real acknowledgement that we’re heading to a future where AI can create a lot of the documents that people used to rely on Office for. Microsoft’s move to bring Office into Copilot has the potential to fundamentally reshape the future of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. Nadella is now positioning Copilot as the platform for this new AI era of work, instead of just cramming AI features into Office itself. Microsoft has tried to sell business on Copilot in Office multiple times in recent years, but the response to a $30 per month, per user Copilot subscription was lukewarm two years ago. Nadella still thinks Microsoft will nail AI at work, and in turn convince businesses to pay for it. “The way we think of Copilot is not just the product itself changing, it’s the contours of work inside the enterprise changing,” said Nadella. [It’s] the dance between the shape of the product and the organizational structural change to work.” The pad * Microsoft refreshes its smaller Surface Pro and Laptop with Qualcomm’s X2 Plus. Microsoft is keeping the same design and hardware features of its existing Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices, but it’s upgrading them with Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon X2 Plus chips. That should mean better performance and battery life, but thanks to RAMageddon, it also means higher price points. Microsoft is also bringing back the black color option for both of these smaller Surface devices, with platinum silver or violet colors available too. Both of these refreshed Surface devices will be available on October 13th, with the 12-inch Surface Pro starting at $1,149.99 and the 13-inch Surface Laptop starting at $1,199.99. * Microsoft’s new Surface Mouse has haptic feedback and a customizable action button. Microsoft’s smaller refreshed Surface devices might not be all that exciting, but the company also announced a refresh to the Surface Mouse for the first time in 10 years. The new model includes haptic feedback support and has a customizable action button for the first time. It’s nice to see more mice with haptic feedback, which works through subtle vibrations during things like clicks, drags, and alignment in Windows 11. * Microsoft Ink Canvas is an AI-powered digital sketchpad. Microsoft is launching a new digital sketchpad app for Windows next month. Microsoft Ink Canvas will be available first on the new Surface Pro 12-inch, and other supported devices on October 13th. It supports sketching with pen or touch, and includes AI image generation and summaries. It’s essentially an AI-powered version of the various digital whiteboard apps Microsoft has created over the years. * Microsoft puts Brad Smith in charge of communications. Microsoft is moving its communications group out of marketing and into its Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs (CELA) organization. The surprise change will see Microsoft vice chair and president Brad Smith oversee communications, while the company searches for a replacement for Frank Shaw, chief communications officer, who is departing later this year. This move seems to position Microsoft PR to be more like how AI startups operate, allowing researchers to lead demos and write blogs. Microsoft is still chasing Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI to become a top AI model lab, and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he’s “excited about the opportunity to help our engineers, sellers, partners, and others closest to our products and customers become an even bigger part of how we tell our story.” * Bill Gates says regulate AI, because it’s powerful enough to cause a billion deaths. While Microsoft is pushing ahead with its new Copilot app, Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates wants AI regulations. In an interview with NBC News, Gates says that AI is “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths.” He wants politicians and law enforcement to “get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like.” * Microsoft is killing off the “Copilot Plus PC” brand. When Microsoft announced its Surface Laptop Ultra in May, there was no Copilot Plus PC branding to be found. Even though the new 12-inch Microsoft Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop technically meet the system requirements for a Copilot Plus PC, Microsoft is not calling them by that name anymore. There doesn’t appear to be a direct replacement after two and a half years of Copilot Plus PCs, but Microsoft does have a Windows event next week, so maybe we’ll hear about a new brand for its AI-focused PCs. * Human workers are reviewing prompts and images sent to Microsoft Copilot. Human contractors are reviewing Copilot users’ prompts and uploaded images, according to a new report from 404 Media. The publication reports that some contractors working on Copilot have described seeing disturbing requests and potentially illegal images. “Faces are always uncensored, and many of the prompts are sexual in nature and dubiously consensual,” says one person who reportedly works on the Copilot prompts. * Xbox’s Mythic Achievements are here, and they’re just like PlayStation Platinum trophies. Microsoft has officially announced its new Xbox Mythic Achievements, and they’re already available for Xbox Insiders to test. Mythic Achievements work a lot like Sony’s PlayStation Platinum trophies and are unlocked once you’ve earned every original achievement for a game. Mythic Achievements leaked as part of an Xbox PC app last week, complete with a unique unlock sound. Mythic Achievements are now in testing just weeks after Xbox CEO Asha Sharma revealed that Xbox would be getting a platinum trophy equivalent later this year. * Windows 11’s 2026 update is now available. Microsoft is rolling out Windows 11 version 26H2, aka the Windows 11 2026 Update. It’s what Microsoft calls a “small enablement package,” allowing Windows 11 users to download and install the latest release quickly with a single restart. So what’s new? Well, due to the way Microsoft releases new Windows features these days, many of the same features that have been rolling out to version 25H2 will be part of 26H2. * Gears of War: E-Day is a great game launching at a terrible time. My colleague Andrew Webster has been playing Gears of War: E-Day, and he’s impressed. “E-Day is reminiscent of a James Cameron film: Absolutely every element is in service to creating a thrilling sci-fi spectacle,” says Webster. “It’s as close to a playable Aliens as you’re bound to find.” * Xbox’s Gears of War pizza cutter sold out in hours. Speaking of Gears of War, Xbox has teamed up with Prince St. Pizza to launch a pizza cutter to mark the launch of E-Day. The $60 cutter is built in the shape of the Prototype Lancer weapon from the game, and also includes an in-game pizza emblem. Unfortunately for Gears of War fans, the cutter sold out within hours of going on sale. Still, Prince St. Pizza will also be selling an “Emergence Pie” pizza with a spicy vodka sauce, so if you’re lucky they might even carve it up for you with the Lancer cutter. * “Xbox is not for sale” says Microsoft’s gaming chief. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has denied reports that Microsoft is considering selling off its Xbox business. “Xbox is not for sale,” says Sharma in an interview with The New York Times. “We will do whatever it takes to set the company up for success, and we will look at the right partnerships, the right operating model and everything needed to achieve that.” The Information reported in June that Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood had been considering spinning out Xbox entirely, and then reported earlier this month that both execs have “more recently supported Sharma’s plans to overhaul the unit.” The overhaul includes moving Halo, Sea of Thieves, and Age of Empires under Activision, as well as selling off smaller Xbox studios. The recent changes look geared toward making Xbox a wholly owned subsidiary like Microsoft has done with LinkedIn. Note: I’m traveling to San Francisco next week for the Windows and Surface event on October 7th, so Notepad might not arrive on time. I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there. Thanks for subscribing to Notepad.

articles.title: Microsoft’s Office and Teams chief is leaving
articles.summary: Ryan Roslansky is leaving after nearly 18 years at LinkedIn and Microsoft.
articles.body: After nearly 18 years at LinkedIn and Microsoft, Ryan Roslansky is leaving the company. Roslansky, who until recently was the CEO of LinkedIn, was promoted to the head of Office last year and then took control of Microsoft Teams earlier this year. Roslansky’s departure has triggered another leadership shuffle inside Microsoft. “Ryan leaves the organization in a strong position,” says Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella in an internal memo. “Over the past year, Ryan’s team has done critical work bringing together the product, engineering, and design foundations that have made this next phase possible.” Roslansky is leaving a week after Microsoft announced its new Copilot, which the company is positioning as “the OS for work.” He’s also leaving around a month after calling fully AI-generated documents “a doom loop” for workers. “If we’re not careful, we’ll end up with a very expensive way to avoid writing and reading in an ocean of sameness, genericness,” said Roslansky in his LinkedIn post. Microsoft is now moving the teams behind Office and Microsoft Teams over to Charles Lamanna, as part of the Copilot, Agents, and Platform (CAP) organization. This is the second major reshuffling of the Office teams after Rajesh Jha, former head of Microsoft’s experiences and devices group, retired from Microsoft earlier this year. Microsoft’s chief design officer, Jon Friedman, is also moving to report to Copilot chief Jacob Andreou. Microsoft appointed Dan Shapero as its LinkedIn CEO earlier this year, and he will continue in this role and report directly to Nadella. Roslansky describes the decision to leave Microsoft as a hard one in his own memo to his teams, and reveals he wasn’t willing to move to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters full time. “I know what it would take for me to lead the next phase of this work well: being in Redmond full time, every day,” says Roslansky. “But my life and my family’s life are here in the Bay Area.” Here’s Roslansky’s memo in full: > Team, > In 1996, as a college freshman, I taught myself to code so a few friends and I could help other students find a place to live around campus. I didn’t know much. I did know the internet was about to change how people found things, and I wanted to be as close to that as possible. > In 2009, Jeff Weiner made me his first hire at LinkedIn. I’ve spent the nearly 18 years since working on a much bigger version of that same idea: helping people find opportunity, and then helping them do great work once they have it. > This has (obviously) been the best professional experience of my life. > As a product manager, I got to build dozens of features that are still around today (some good, some not so good!). When I became CEO in 2020, the world was months into a pandemic that changed what work even meant. Nobody hands you a playbook for that. This team wrote one anyway. Since then, LinkedIn has passed a billion members and nearly tripled its business, and every bit of that belongs to the people who built it. > Last year, Satya asked me to help build the future of M365. Once again, the old rules didn’t apply. AI was rapidly changing how professionals work, and the world’s largest productivity suite needed to lead the way. That meant figuring out what Copilot, and the future of work, should look like as one ecosystem. > We still have a ways to go, but the progress over the past year has been inspiring to watch. A lot of talented people set aside their own roadmaps to make that happen. Thank you. I know it wasn’t easy. > Satya, thank you. When LinkedIn joined Microsoft, you gave us room to build, and then trusted many of us with a lot more. I’ve learned more from you than I can fit in an email, and I’m grateful for the friendship that came with it. > All of which made this a hard decision. I know what it would take for me to lead the next phase of this work well: being in Redmond full time, every day. But my life and my family’s life are here in the Bay Area. My wife Leigh gives her time to more local organizations than I can keep track of. Our youngest daughter just started high school, and our dog Buddy remains deeply committed to the trails on the Peninsula! > I thought about this for a long time. It’s the right call. The work now goes to leaders who are set up to take it further. I can’t wait to see what they do with it. > Over the years, people have asked me what’s kept me so energized and motivated in this work. I think the answer is that I got to spend my career working where doing good and doing well are the same thing. In technology, that’s the best place to operate. > Most companies start by focusing on doing well, so doing good becomes a compromise. It’s the last slide of the PowerPoint, or a separate .org. But when doing good is built into the product itself, it becomes a real competitive advantage. When we build valuable products, people find jobs, they hire, they learn skills, they start companies, they run companies. That creates value for members, customers and the world. And for our business too. > Not many companies get to work this way, and not many people get the chance to build something like it. We do. > That matters more now than it ever has. Technology will continue to touch every job on the planet, and the people building it will decide what kind of world it helps create. I can’t think of a better group to figure that out than the people reading this note. > Thank you for the best 18 years I could have asked for. RR

articles.title: Make unknown callers explain why they're calling
articles.summary: iPhone, Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy phones now offer call screening that asks unknown callers to identify themselves before your phone rings.
articles.body: You know the feeling. Your phone rings, you look down and see a number you do not recognize. Now you have to decide whether to answer or let it go to voicemail. That choice gets harder when you are expecting a call from a doctor, repair person or someone else who may not be in your contacts. Fortunately, your phone can now help figure out who is on the other end before you get involved. With iOS 27, your iPhone can ask an unknown caller for their name and why they are calling. Google Pixel phones have their own Call Screen feature. Compatible Samsung Galaxy phones can also use AI-powered call screening. Here is how each one works on the latest software. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better healthcare. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare With AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com ANDROID FAKE CALL DETECTION WARNS YOU ABOUT SCAMS How to screen unknown callers on iPhone Apple's Call Screening feature can automatically answer calls from unknown numbers without interrupting you. The caller gets asked for their name and the reason for the call. After they respond, your iPhone rings and shows you what they said. That gives you a little more information before deciding whether to answer. How to turn on Call Screening on iPhone Once you turn it on, calls from unknown numbers are asked for more information before your iPhone rings. Apple also gives you two other options in the same section. Never turn Call Screening off. Silence sends calls from unsaved numbers directly to voicemail and keeps them in your Recents list. For many people, Ask Reason for Calling may offer a useful middle ground. You can still hear from someone important without immediately answering every unfamiliar number. You can filter suspected spam calls too While you are in the Phone settings, you can also review Apple's call filtering options. Go to Settings → Apps → Phone, then scroll to the call filtering section. Turning on Spam lets your carrier identify potential spam or fraud calls. Those calls can then be silenced, sent to voicemail and moved into the Spam list. You can also turn on Unknown Callers. That moves calls from unknown numbers out of your main Recents list and into a separate Unknown Callers list. FAKE VERIZON FRAUD CALL NEARLY STOLE HIS ACCOUNT How Samsung Galaxy screens unknown calls Samsung has also brought call screening to compatible Galaxy phones. Samsung says the feature is available on supported Galaxy phones running One UI 8.5 or later. However, feature availability can still vary by Galaxy model, carrier and region. Galaxy Call screening can answer the caller and ask why they are calling. You can then read the caller's response as a live transcription. How to turn on Call screening on Samsung Galaxy Samsung also lets you choose a transcription language and customize the assistant's voice. If you prefer to decide which calls get screened, you can do that manually. When an incoming call appears, tap Call assist, then tap Call screening. The AI assistant answers for you and asks the caller to state the purpose of the call. Their response then appears as text on your screen. If you do not see Call screening, check for the latest Galaxy software update. You should also make sure the Samsung Phone app is current. Some Galaxy models may not support the feature. How to screen unknown calls on a Google Pixel Google Pixel phones take a slightly different approach with Call Screen. The feature can answer certain calls for you and ask the caller why they are calling. Depending on your Pixel and settings, Google can also screen some calls automatically. How to turn on Call Screen on Pixel On newer Pixel phones, you may see Maximum protection, Medium protection and Basic protection. Medium protection is Google's recommended setting and screens suspicious calls while declining known spam. Maximum protection screens unknown numbers more aggressively, while Basic protection mainly declines known spam. You can still screen a call manually. When an unfamiliar number comes in, tap Screen call. Call Assist will ask who is calling and why while you watch the response appear as a live transcript. From there, you can answer the call, hang up or use one of the suggested responses. Why screening can beat automatically silencing every unknown caller Sending every unfamiliar number straight to voicemail certainly cuts down on interruptions. However, it can also send legitimate callers there. Maybe you are waiting for a medical office to call from a number you have never seen. Perhaps a service technician needs to reach you from a work phone. Call screening gives that person a chance to explain why they are trying to reach you. You can then make the call about whether to answer. There is also a security benefit. Scam callers often count on getting someone on the phone quickly. Screening puts another step between the caller and you. However, do not assume someone is legitimate simply because they answered the screening question. Scammers can still lie about who they are. Caller ID can also be spoofed. Do not let a convincing answer lower your guard Call screening gives you information. It does not verify someone's identity. If a caller claims to represent your bank or another company and suddenly asks for money or login information, end the call. The same advice applies if someone asks for a one-time security code. Instead, contact the organization yourself through its official app or website. For financial accounts, you can also use the phone number printed on your card or statement. This is especially important because phone scams continue to get more convincing. Scammers can spoof familiar numbers and create a sense of urgency to push you into acting quickly. Kurt's key takeaways I like the idea of making an unknown caller explain themselves before they get my attention. With iOS 27, iPhone owners can have unfamiliar callers provide a name and reason before the phone rings. Pixel owners can use Google's Call Screen, while compatible Galaxy phones offer their own call screening feature. For me, screening makes more sense than automatically silencing every unfamiliar number. There are plenty of legitimate reasons someone outside your contacts may need to reach you. Still, treat the screening response as information rather than proof. If the conversation turns to passwords, money or account access, hang up and contact the company yourself. Would you rather have your phone screen every unknown caller first, or do you still prefer sending unfamiliar numbers straight to voicemail? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: Android Central ‘will continue’ despite laying off its staff
articles.summary: Android Central, a blog focused on the Android ecosystem, laid off its staff yesterday, but site owner Future confirms to The Verge that the site will continue publishing.
articles.body: Android Central, a blog focused on the Android ecosystem, laid off its staff yesterday, but owner Future confirms to The Verge that the site will continue publishing. Yesterday, four of the six staffers on Android Central’s staff page posted publicly about the layoffs, including Shruti Shekar, Derrek Lee, Harish Jonnalagadda, and Nicholas Sutrich, and former senior editor Namerah Saud Fatmi updated her LinkedIn to indicate that her tenure at Android Central had ended. Both Lee, the site’s managing editor, and Sutrich confirmed that all remaining staff were laid off. The former staffers weren’t told whether the site would shut down. Today, new posts have been published to the site, though are from the site’s freelance contributors rather than the previous full-time staffers. “Future will continue to publish Android Central. We’ll share further information about the future of the site in due course,” Future spokesperson Nicole Martineau tells The Verge, adding: “We will not be providing any further comment at this time.” Android Police, another Android-focused blog, also laid off at least two staffers recently. The site currently lists an editorial team of four people. Valnet, which owns Android Police and previously purchased The Verge’s sister site Polygon, didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
